entries.body:
Got stuck in Loganville for the weekend — the weather was awful — it blew & rained on Saturday, then rained all Sunday. The Rally hype was intense — all these boaters talking themselves into going to sea. Talked to Tranquility & Silverfin Monday morning — they were in Peterson Bay so we went up there. There we finally met Indulgence II with Mike, Elke and Ben; also Julia with Larry & Ken; and Overproof with Virginia & Derek. We had seen these boats since Fiji!

Brian was happy to hang out with Ben, or Larry from Julia, those guys are big boys! We had a wonderful time there, dinghying to the Blue Hole, diving the crashed airplane on the reef, partying with the other boats. Just before they were planning to leave for Australia last Thursday, Ben was jumping off our spreaders with Brian, slipped, and fell on the life lines, gashed his head on the toerail. He looked pretty beat up at first. Got an ambulance and got him to the hospital. Luckily, he only needed some stitches in his forehead. He was back the next day, feeling fine. So, we stayed too, spent a lot of time with Indulgence & Julia.

Finally got out of Peterson Bay on Monday, went down to Palikulo Bay. Had a blast exploring the freighter beached there, swimming in the clear water. Hung out with Carl & Kathleen on Silverfin for the day. Hated to leave! But it is time to go on now — 2 weeks of light winds ahead and Chesterfield Reef beckoned. We have 10–12 knots of wind from the SE, we are still sailing along the south coast of Espiritu Santo. Goodbye Vanuatu — it has been a memorable two months!
entries.conditions: Departed Luganville / Palikulo for Australia via Chesterfield. Wind: SE 10–12 knots.

entries.body: Well it could be worse! Last night was peaceful after we poled out the genoa, moving at 4½ knots, wind backed to the east. This morning the wind almost died completely, we were bouncing along at 1½ knots for a while. Not thrilling, but better than nothing. The wind came back this afternoon, 8–10 knots and we are moving smoothly at 5 knots with four sails up. Nice sailing! We expected very light winds for this trip, want to get to Chesterfield and enjoy a few calm days there before the last leg back to a continent.
entries.conditions: Wind: east then light, later 8–10 knots; 5 knots with four sails. 24-hour run — 105 miles.

entries.body: Beautiful night last night, charging along up to 6 knots at times with 4 sails up, following the path made by the extremely bright crescent moon. It was quite comfortable — we are all enjoying this sail. Talked to Indulgence & Julia this morning. Lost a big fish along with the lure, Thomas is hungry for something different. He ate enough oysters and coconut crabs in Peterson Bay!
entries.conditions: Up to 6 knots with 4 sails. 24-hour run — 115 miles.

entries.body: Another nice night, but sunrise brought light winds. It was hot, progress slow, boat didn't steer well. Finally got a bit more wind late in afternoon. Caught a huge mahi just after sunrise.
entries.conditions: Light winds after sunrise. 24-hour run — 117 miles.

entries.body:
Not a very exciting day — been almost becalmed most of it. Trying to get the boat going again now, before sunset. Morale is good, however!

Oh — had some hitch hikers last night! A tired booby landed on the mizzen boom just after sunset. He was no problem — his ass was hanging over the water, but then his buddies landed on the spreaders and all of a sudden there was bird shit all over the place. Thomas chased them off, but the first one stayed until sunrise.
Today is flat calm, oily sea, totally hazy gray horizon, no visibility. We play with the sails and then get tired of it. Very hot, good day to do laundry!

Wind came back late yesterday afternoon with a bang! Within an hour we had the main down, mizzen reefed, furled genoa. It blew like stink all night — 30–35 knots from the south. It was relatively calm north of Chesterfield Reef, which we passed in the middle of the night. No stopping at uncharted reefs in this weather! Finally switched to staysail to try to slow the boat down. Overproof and Indulgence II got nailed too, after us. Very uncomfortable ride — food flying all over the place. Being becalmed sounds good now! Will head to Frederick Reef now and stop there.
entries.conditions: Wind: S 30–35 knots; passed Chesterfield Reef at night. 24-hour run — 135 miles.

entries.body: Today has been an exhilarating day — blue sky, big waves, lots of whitecaps. 30 knots of wind. Keep trying to slow the boat down, it is impossible. Running 5½–6 under staysail only. Not so uncomfortable as yesterday. It is possible to stand on deck without getting wet. We will be at Frederick Cay Reef before sunrise tomorrow. Looking forward to peaceful anchorage in clear blue water, a sandy beach.
entries.conditions: Wind: 30 knots; 5½–6 under staysail. Bound Frederick Reef. 24-hour run — 145 miles.

entries.body: Arrived at Frederick Reef Thurs at sunrise, anchored just before the Namba Net at 8 am. Not exactly a calm anchorage! The boat pitched and rolled, too rough to get off or swim, still blowing 20+. We had reduced to bare poles before sunrise and were still doing 3–4 knots. Indulgence II arrived at 10pm, rather frazzled from navigating into the reef in the dark. Had a fun day yesterday — hanging out on the coral rubble hump that stuck out of the sea at high tide, then had beers and dinner on Indulgence. Figured out a new way to hoist the dinghy aboard last night, with the staysail halyard. Left at 7 this morning, 15–20 SE wind, hard on it heading 195° to Bundaberg. It's a beautiful day; just wish the wind was more easterly. As long as it stays where it is and we can hold the course, no problem.
entries.conditions: Frederick Reef layover; departed for Bundaberg. Wind: SE 15–20, hard on it, course 195°.

entries.body: What a nice night, full moon, light winds, calm seas, very comfortable. We made lots of southing, can just hold our course today. Were doing 7 knots for awhile! Hope the wind holds & doesn't turn more south.
entries.conditions: Light winds; up to 7 knots. 24-hour run — 140 miles.

stops.name: Bundaberg, Fraser Island & Tin Can Bay

entries.body:
We arrived in Bundaberg Monday morning at sunrise, had to slow down some once we passed the reef. There were 20 boats ahead of us awaiting checkin! Got through by 4pm, piece of cake. Relaxed with Indulgence II. Bundaberg river entrance was not particularly thrilling — very flat, ugly gray water, poisonous sea snakes. We went up river to the town with Virginia on Overproof for a few days, to do some shopping. Bundaberg was neat and clean, everything available. The men walk around in Crocodile Dundee outfits, and the women are scantily dressed. Very redneck. Spent a couple more days at the mouth of the river, until Julia with Ken & Larry showed up. Left Mon the 17th for Fraser Island — what a great spot! It was paradise there — miles of white sand beaches, crystal clear water, birds. But the wind turned NW and we had to get out. Too bad — it would have been perfect for windsurfing in the lagoon. Spent the next few days traveling south in the Great Sandy Straits. Great sailing in flat water, but the NW winds made anchoring uncomfortable. Finally found some protection in Gary's Anchorage. Came down to Tin Can Bay yesterday, just before the wind turned south again. Anchored in the river here, quite a way from town, but it's peaceful. Lots of sand bars, sleepy little town. Overproof is here, mostly Aussie boats. Will be stuck until wind turns NE again.

Bundaberg highlights: nasty thick gray sea snakes, 1000's of bats flying across the river at sunset. Yucky water!
entries.conditions: Arrived Bundaberg; later Fraser Island, Great Sandy Strait, Garry's Anchorage (written Gary's), Tin Can Bay. Wind: NW then south.

entries.body: Enjoyed our week in Tin Can Bay — we met Virginia on Overproof there and she arranged a trip to a National Forest and a hike to Lake Boona with some friends of hers. It was beautiful — huge old Kauri trees towering out of sight, thousands of birds. I had a refreshing swim in the fresh water lake. Tin Can Bay was very quiet, but people were friendly, and internet at the library was free. The dinghy ride was a bit long and wet. Mostly only Australian boats around. We spent one day at Inskip Point, and walked part of the endless windward beach. Today we left at 4:30 to sail down to Mooloolaba, 60 miles. Not a lot of wind in the morning, but it picked up to 15 in the afternoon. The bar crossing to offshore was crazy — 20 boats next to each other, motoring through 6ft swells, trying to get out. What a zoo! But of course eventually they all passed Charlotte. We got in and were anchored by 4, found a nice hole to sit in. Very suburban here — fancy huge holiday houses along the waterfront.
entries.conditions: Tin Can Bay via Inskip Point to Mooloolaba, 60 miles. Wind light then 15; rough bar exit.

entries.body: A month went by quickly in Mooloolaba! I guess we were comfortable there. It took a while to get used to the scene, but we enjoyed afternoons on the beach, with Brian on his boogie board. He really got into it! Suleika with Martin, Katherine and 8-yr-old [illegible], showed up, so we decided to spend Christmas with them. It was a fun day, spent time on the beach as usual. Brian drove us crazy wanting things. Got into exercising every morning, running, working out at an exercise site. Silent Runner came through a few days before Christmas, also Tranquility. We went to the Australia Zoo and saw crocodiles, kangaroos, and koalas, also many snakes, poisonous & pythons. We saw the last Lord of the Rings movie. Got used to the yuppie-tourist atmosphere but then the water cops came around and bugged us to move on. Indulgence & Julia arrived, but they were disappointing — too involved in each other. It was a fun month, but time to move on. Today winds are light and we took all day to get 40 miles south to Tangalooma, on Moreton Island. We saw Desert Rose sailing north to Mooloolaba — what a shame to miss them by a day!
entries.conditions: After ~1 month at Mooloolaba; sailed ~40 miles to Tangalooma, Moreton Island. Light winds.

entries.body:
After a morning of school work, we decided to move on as the anchorage was getting rolly. Today is great sailing — downwind with the genoa poled out. Only 20 miles to Peel Island where we will wait out the NW flow. We meet up with Virginia on Overproof here — lots of boats, but it is a big bay, long sandy beach. Thomas is trying windsurfing here.

p.s. — New Years Eve in Mooloolaba was fantastic — lots of fireworks on the beach, some in a boat out on the water. It was a sight with the lights on the crashing surf, fireworks shooting into the waves. The Australians worked very hard at getting drunk, what a scene.
entries.conditions: Tangalooma to Peel Island, ~20 miles. Downwind, genoa poled out; waiting out NW flow.

entries.body:
Lots of catching up to do! We arrived at the Spit in Southport on Sun Jan 11, after a fun weekend at Dux anchorage, on northern South Stradbroke, where we met members of the Southport Yacht Club. Saw lots of wallabies there, beautiful beach with perfect sand dunes. We were appalled when we first dropped the hook in Southport, high rise buildings dotting the skyline. But the Spit was very pretty, with the beach right next to the boat and the ocean not far away. And there were kid boats!

We really enjoyed Manuhiri, a Kiwi ferro boat with Shawn, Angie and their kids Alex, Rory, and Nikki. Brian became special buddies with all 3 of them. Silent Sound, Canadian with Ray, Stella, boys Bradley & Harry, stayed for a month. Brian and Bradley became quite good friends and made up a game together.

Then there were the Aussie boats. La Passorala with Les, Colleen, Jordan & Amy. Keemar III with Bruce, Robin, Jackson & Ryan, 2 big goofy boys that Brian had a lot of fun with. The kids had fires on the beach at night and had a life of their own. I enjoyed watching Brian interact — he has good people skills. Thomas did a lot of wind surfing — figured out water starts and jibes in the flat water behind the sandbars. We enjoyed friendship, happy hours on the beach, lots of swimming & beach walks. Found a small python, called a carpet snake, on the path down to the beach — he would come out at evening, just before sundown. Rick & Mary on Tranquility pulled in and stayed.

It was hard to leave — we felt part of a community for a change. After much agonizing about what to do with our lives, we decided to sail directly back to the U.S., unless plans change of course! So, it is time to move on and we are on our way back to Mooloolaba, to take care of some things, provision, and then on to the Great Barrier Reef. We have enjoyed the fantastic weather, sand and surf of Australia, and Aussie English sounds normal to us now!
entries.conditions: Catch-up entry: Southport Spit stay from mid-January; departing north toward Mooloolaba / GBR.

entries.body: Spent 2 lovely days at the Sand Hills anchorage on south Moreton Island. We climbed the huge sand dunes that went on, ridge after ridge. It was like a desert, nothing to see but sand in the middle. Today we had a fast and rolly sail up to Mooloolaba. Charlotte really got moving, downwind in 20 knots. The bar at Mooloolaba was exciting— we came in between the buoys and the breakers. It is nice to be here again — there was a bike race downtown we watched. Thomas was happy with his boat’s performance today!

How easy to spend 2 weeks in Mooloolaba! Brian spent a weekend with Ben on Indulgence and was at the beach boogie-boarding every day. Saw Suleika with Katherine, Martin & Will. Then La Passarola with Les, Colleen, Jordan & Amy, came up from Southport, also [Quolle] with Tim, Trish and boys Matthew & David. We had a barbeque in the park. Did lots of walking as usual. Today we left at sunrise, back to Wide Bay Bar, retracing our path to the north of Fraser Island. Very rolly, big swell, Charlotte happy with 20 knots, we have to slow the boat down to time a low tide arrival. The bar was breaking all across when we arrived, kind of scary but we made it through. Anchored right next to a sand bank — wondered why the birds were making such a racket in the dark.
Happy Easter! Cruising up the Sandy Straits today, in company with Passarola. Nice sunny day, calm seas, much nicer than yesterday!

Spent one last evening with La Passarola at White Cliffs anchorage. Today we left early, motored 2 hours in light wind, then sailed north at 2 knots for hours. Finally out into Hervey Bay open waters at 2pm and doing 4 knots with mizzen drifter up. Guess we will continue all night to Lady Musgrave Reef. Nice weather, calm seas.

Arrived at Lady Musgrave Tuesday morning. Had a calm day [there], cleaned the bottom, I did some snorkeling. Pretty colors on the reef, violet, periwinkle, baby blue, bright yellow, electric blue. Caught a mackerel approaching the reef, so Thomas and Brian ate well. Wednesday the wind was up, they did some windsurfing. Beautiful shades of blue over the lagoon! Now we are sailing to Pancake Creek on the mainland, a 35-mile sail. Nice 10 knot wind, some swell, not rolling too much.

Pancake Creek was interesting, would have liked to walk the sandbars and explore the island. However we got underway at 5 am, still dark now that it is no longer summer! Having a great sail today, 20 knots, dead downwind, 5½–6 knots boat speed. Heading for Great Keppel Island, an ambitious 65-mile run. We just crossed the Tropic of Capricorn, which passes through Cape Capricorn. Back in the tropics!

Rolled all night at Great Keppel Island. So now we are underway again, but spirits are low. All we want is a nice place to spend a day or 2. It would be nice to walk again. The next good anchorage is over 200 miles away. Winds light today, guess we will stop at Port Clinton and see what the wind will do.

Today is a much happier day! We spent a quiet night at Port Clinton — but were inundated by gnats in the morning. We left with light east winds, which have continued all day. It is slow going, but the sun is warm and the swells are down. More comfortable than some anchorages! I guess we will continue overnight to Scawfell Island.

The wind was so light yesterday we finally gave up and motored to High Peak for the night. We weren't the only ones to make only 35 miles today. But at least Thomas gets a mackerel for dinner every day! Had a quiet evening and set off again today. Once again light winds but it is comfortable enough out here. The hottest day we have had in a while. Only 3 knots average but I guess it's better than sitting still.

It has been an interesting sail the past week among the rocky islands. At times the current grips our keel so hard we can barely go forward. Even now, there are whitecaps and we seem to be making good progress, but the GPS shows speed hardly 4 knots. We never seem to have the current with us, only against us. We had a pleasant night with some good sailing at times. We are under full main, poled-out genoa, yankee and mizzen; we still can't maintain 5 knots. But we have done 3, and we will anchor this evening at Goldsmith Island, in sight of the Whitsundays. The weather is tropical again — we are at 20° latitude. Feels great!

Still in the Whitsundays. We sailed Wed to Cid Harbor on Whitsunday Island. It was a calm comfortable stop, small rocky beach with a brook; We walked in the woods some, got scared by big gnarly-looking spiders! Then sailed 15 miles to Airlie Beach to get fresh food — good vegetable market on Saturday morning. We enjoyed the fresh water lagoon in the middle of town. Looked at some incredible opals in a local store. This morning, in the squally rainy weather, we sailed out to Hook Island. Sitting on a mooring now, in the rain, pretty place with steep rocky hillside, clear blue water. Will go out to the reef at Bird Island when the weather clears.

Hook Island was nice, we enjoyed the convenience of a mooring. Never did get to go snorkeling, the boys refused to go. It was busy with charter boats. Today the sun shone, so of course we had to leave! Light winds so we sailed to Gloucester Passage to await the wind change forecasted for tomorrow.

Spent yesterday in Gloucester Passage, moved around a bit when the wind turned west. Light wind and lots of rain. Left this morning with 20–25 SW, great sailing for a while, 6–7 knots on a reach. Of course it didn't last and now we are underway again, after a total wind stall, light NE winds. At least we are pointed in the right direction. It was quite nice sailing for some time. Destination the Palm Islands north of Townsville.

Happy May Day! It is quite an enjoyable day out here so we decided to continue on to Cairns. 15 knots from the south, so we are poled out, rolling along. Supposed to blow 20–25 the next 3 days so we want to get in. Lots of islands sticking out everywhere, a lot of cargo traffic.

Sailing along the NE Queensland coast, Thomas says it is hard to believe there are 7 billion people in the world. The hills are rougher and more jagged here. Hinchinbrook Island looks quite forbidding from sea. It is hard to believe that all the reefs of the Great Barrier Reef are just a few miles to windward. The channel is much narrower here, 5–10 miles wide. Lots of cargoes, all on the same path as us. Why do we see them mostly at night? The night sails have been calm, if a bit frustrating, with constant wind changes. The air is warm, you can actually sit in the cockpit and be marginally comfortable. Today we are flying along, poled out, at 6–7 knots in 15–20 knots of wind. The current has been in our favor the past two days. We plan to drop anchor late this afternoon in Mission Bay, just east of Cairns harbor. Cairns will be a time of making more decisions — oh horror! But I think we had enjoyed these 2½ days at sea and the time for reflection they have afforded.

Two weeks in Cairns, we were glad to get away, although we liked the city. Hauled out and painted the bottom at the Cairns Cruising Yacht Club. People were all very friendly and helpful. There was a nice lagoon downtown, but unfortunately it closed for repairs. I enjoyed the free morning exercise classes — took one on Pilates and tai chi. The Pilates is for me! I splurged and bought myself an opal ring. We ran into Soya — Roger & Vipa — on the dock. They were traveling by car and took us for a drive to Port Douglas and up on the mountain. Got burned out on shopping centers — we have seen too many in Australia! But finally other cruising boats caught up with us and we had an evening onshore with Tom & Liz on Feel Free and Chris & Mandy on Bedouin. Left Cairns Tuesday morning for Michaelmas Cay where we enjoyed some fantastic snorkeling — incredibly alive reefs with bright blue elkhorn coral, tons of colorful reef fish, and a bunch of giant blue-lipped clams. They are so weird — I had fun messing with them, trying to get them to close — and they do, even though their shells look as though they could never move again. The little sand cay was home to thousands of birds who made a constant nonstop racket, even at night. The tourist boats were quiet and didn't really bother us. This morning we headed for Low Islands, 27 miles away. Great sailing inside the Barrier Reef, Charlotte averaged over 6 knots today in 20–25 knots. That makes Thomas happy. Spanish does not make Brian happy, I am afraid. I am very happy to be swimming and snorkeling again. It feels like we are finally cruising.

Another smooth fast sail! The wind was down this morning, much more comfortable in 15–20 knots. By the time we reached Hope Islands, it was honking again. Low Isle didn't thrill us, tourist boats, huts on the beach, murky green water — probably due to the mangroves — and a whole fleet of fishing boats. But Thomas had caught another mackerel and we barbequed it on Bedouin with Chris & Mandy. This place has no tourists, lots of coral, a pristine sandy beach.

Once again we are flying up the reef — 6–7 knots in 20–25 K. Spent 2 pleasant days at Hope Island, walked around on the beach, cleaned the bottom. Nasty barnacles from Cairns, even after a new paint job. The reefs looked great, but the water was disappointingly murky. Guess we will go into Cooktown for a day or two.

We spent a pleasant afternoon wandering around Cooktown, although it rained almost constantly. Lots of Captain Cook memorabilia. The anchorage was a bit tight and all the locals stared at us from the docks. Moved on this morning to Lizard Island! The first leg was to windward — don't understand how Captain Cook ever got out of there! It is blowing 20–25 as usual and with wind forward of the beam, not so comfortable. We sailed up to the lagoon anchorage at Lizard but there were no boats there. But Watsons Bay is quite nice.

Finally tore ourselves away from Lizard Island, had a great time there. Nice bunch of cruisers, including Feel Free with Liz & Tom, niece Tracy who lives in Atlanta; Bedouin, the Dutch boats Ciris and Borache, Tranquility, South African Just Jinx, English Astrika. We hiked to Cook's Lookout with a breathtaking view of the lagoon. We hiked to the lagoon with our snorkel gear and dove the reefs out there, we looked at huge fish and giant clams. Brian had fun with all the people, no time to play computer games! Monday we did the tour of the research station. Every night we had happy hour on the beach. Lots of walking, swimming, diving and socializing. There was even a well with a hand pump so I could do laundry every day! Time passed quickly. It was a magic spot. But today we moved on, 30 miles to Howick Island. Fast sailing as usual.

Another good run — 52 miles to Stanley Island in the Flinders Group. In company with Feel Free and Tranquility. We were the leaders and stayed that way all day — what a thrill! The boat has been really going well lately — must be the current. Cape Melville was very rough with a confused sea. Anchored by 2:30, great day but a lot of work sailing a ketch!

Spent an extra day in the Flinders group, as we had trouble finding the cave paintings. Friday we started our assault overland in company with Feel Free, Bedouin, and Buccaneer. We stumbled over boulders and through bushes, got bitten by green ants, and finally abandoned our quest to get to the rock where the aboriginal paintings were. Instead we decided to climb a hill that had a WWII radar emplacement at the top. Never found it but had a great view of the islands in the Flinders Group. That afternoon Tranquility joined us and told us how to get to the paintings. So Saturday morning we all piled on Bedouin to try again. We anchored in Owens Channel and took the dinghies across. The paintings were fantastic and awe-inspiring — the first authentic thing we have seen in Australia. But the dinghy ride back was scary — big swells in the channels with the current. Today what a sail! We had Tranquility and Bedouin behind us all the way. Started out light, but picked up to 20 and we were charging along at 7.5 knots on a broad reach. The other boats could never catch up with us. I jumped in the water as soon as we arrived — no crocs here! Everyone enjoyed the day!

Had a lay day at Morris — it is my last chance to swim — and Thomas was hoping to windsurf but the wind just wasn't quite right. We did have a nice long walk on the sand bars that uncovered at low tide and was astonished at the prolific numbers of sea stars burying themselves in the sand as the tide went out. Today is a long — 60 miles — sail to Portland Roads. Bedouin took most of the day to catch up with us. Anchored by 2pm and everyone will enjoy fresh yellow fin tuna for dinner, thanks to Feel Free.

Sailing 42 miles to Margaret Bay around Cape Grenville. We will celebrate Brian's birthday with the group tonight since it is a short day. Winds are up there as usual, 20–25 knots we are getting so used to making 6 knots or more average. The only boat that can pass us, with our hour headstart, is Bedouin. Tranquility is the same speed, Feel Free at 51' is faster but they sail conservatively. The last 2 mornings have been spectacular, sun rising and moon still shining bright in the sky. Brian got one of his new Game Boy games today, so he is content.

Had happy hour and birthday cake on the beach last night with Bedouin & Feel Free, then dinner on Tranquility. Wanted to make Brian spend the night in a small but comfortable cave on the beach as his manhood rite-of-passage, but for some reason, he was not amenable! Dinner on Tranquility was delicious and cozy. After a calmer beginning to the day with a beautiful double rainbow, we are having to reef down again. A lot more rolly today. Brian got presents from Bedouin & Feel Free, plus another Game Boy game — he is alternating between the 2, wishing he had cheats. Destination Bushy Islet today. Bedouin left early to go through Albany Passage in one day.

Bye-bye Pacific Ocean! We had a pleasant walk on Bushy Islet sandbar in the afternoon yesterday. Saw our first croc tracks and assisted a baby turtle who was disoriented on the rocks. Brian let him go in the shallow lagoon. Rather uncomfortable night, pitching and rolling. The sailing today wasn't much better, we were down to a bit of jib poled out and a staysail. Didn't want to reach Albany Passage before 3pm. There was still a current running out and standing seas when we arrived. So Bushy Islet was our last South Pacific and Great Barrier Reef island, tomorrow we enter the Arafura Sea. Calm anchorage here in Albany Pass at Shallow Bay, although the currents and wind gusts are spinning us in circles on anchor. Can't forget the highlight of the day — we spotted a baby crocodile swimming toward our boat, then he turned away when he saw he could not get aboard. About 2 feet long, he was light brown in color and very strong in the big seas.

Last day of day sailing for now — we are burnt out! Calm morning, sailing in the lee of Cape York. We round York Island and officially leave the Pacific. The current pulled us through the pass at Possession Island. Great sailing to windward in flat seas. Bamaga harbor is picturesque, with sandy beaches and palm trees. Bedouin is here, Tranquility & Just Jinx arrive later. We are looking forward to resting for a day.

Had a little happy hour on the beach last night with Feel Free, Bedouin, Tranquility, and Just Jinx. Walked to Bamaga the day before, not much happening, a quiet, neat aborigine village. The only highlight was the opening of the liquor store at 4 pm — all the trucks in the vicinity were there to pick up one case of beer, all they are allowed! The terrain was different — red clay soil, tall grasses, eucalyptus trees. Left for Gove this morning with a light SSE wind, but now it has died completely. The Gulf of Carpentaria is very rolly, short seas.

stops.name: Gulf of Carpentaria
stops.passage: Cape York to the Northern Territory

entries.body: Brilliant night, the wind picked up after dark, the seas were calm, the stars shining brightly and we were charging along at 7 knots for hours. By morning the seas were up, but still not too uncomfortable. We have maintained 6 knots, under full sails now, 15–20 knots, broad reaching. Great sailing!.

Got hammered last night — 25–35 knots, and continuing today. Finally took the mainsail down at sunrise. All we can do is lie around today, with beam seas breaking over the boat. Now we are on the final approach, motor-sailing into it, what fun. Hope Gove is worth it. At least we have sailed fast, we were halfway between Bedouin and Tranquility this morning. Charlotte can really move in the wind!

The ALCAN bauxite mine tour was the highlight of our stay in Gove. The effort they put into reforesting the land and restoring it to its original state was commendable. The aborigines harvest fruit and seeds from the indigenous plant life, dry them, mix them with fertilizer and reseed when the strip mining is finished. Only difference was that the land was about 10 feet lower after mining. I also enjoyed a long swim in the Olympic-sized pool in the town, I had it all to myself. The final 15 miles approach to Gove was horrible — motorsailing in gale-force winds and the last 2 miles was agony, making hardly any headway. But it was worth it to drop the hook! Today the winds are light so we are taking advantage of it to get over to the English Company Islands, 25 miles away. Slow sailing, 4 knots, but it's been 2 months since we have seen winds under 20. We had fun sailing through the 2 cuts between the island groups. Islands are rocky, forbidding looking, very desolate.

Set off at 9am to catch the tides at the next pass through the Wessel Islands, wind picked up to 30–35 by the time we got there. Fun surfing in the waves! Then we close reached another 18 miles up the island to Jensen Bay. It is fantastic here — clear water, sand dunes, rocks to climb on. Charlotte did well going to windward with staysail & reefed main.

Three days passed quickly at Jensen Bay. It was magical there, clear water, lots of fresh water on the island, tiny waterfalls down the rocky cliffs. Fidelio pulled in, we enjoyed catching up with Ian & Ann. Feel Free came down and we had a fun trek across the island to find a waterfall and some caves. The GPS got us there! Along with Astrika, Just Jinx & Bedouin, we had some big happy hours. Now we are out here, rolling like crazy in less than 10 knots of wind. Rather uncomfortable, but I guess we should be glad it's not howling. Saw a big school of very small dolphins earlier, they were light gray & white in color. Caught a big wahoo. The rain seems to be clearing, maybe we will get some steady wind soon. Down to 3 knots, Fidelio passed us with their new sails. Bound for Port Essington or somewhere around Cape Don, en route to Darwin.

It was a great night, perfect sailing. The wind picked up after dark, the seas straightened out and we flew along. Just had trouble sleeping. Today is ideal — 15–20 knots SE, clear blue sky, relatively flat sailing with 4 sails up, poled out genoa and yankee forward. Fidelio is to the north of us, Just Jinx just south, and Tranquility farther to the south. It's kind of fun to see all these sails!

Rather bleary-eyed when I had to run the Sheila net this morning! The wind died last night until 2 am so we motored for several hours. The 4 boats were in sight the whole night. Saw meteors streaking across the sky. Decided not to go into Port Essington with Tranquility and Fidelio, rather continued on to Alcaro Bay with Just Jinx. As usual the final approach was painful, dead into the wind. The Northern Territories have been trying cruising! But it is nice here, a long sandy beach, supposed to be lots of crocs, and Cape Don is just around the corner. Almost finished with Australia, just the final haul to Darwin left.

Just dropped anchor in Darwin Harbor after an overnight sail from Cape Don. Wonderful calm sail last night — to windward in 10 knots, no seas, current with us, dodging reefs with CMap. Had a big party at Alcaro Bay with Just Jinx (John & Verna) and Weiss World. Walked 5K to the lighthouse, and were chased away as soon as we arrived. We are happy to have finally made it to Darwin — it's been a long 3 months of travel. At the gateway to the Indian Ocean. Now of course the boys want to rush to town. Ended up with Fidelio even though we didn't start with them.

Goodbye Australia! We are watching the low land slip away as we sail west, bound for Bali via Ashmore Reef. It was a fun & busy 2 weeks in Darwin. Got to see so many old friends, and say a final goodbye to them as very few are going our way to South Africa this year. Big reunion with Infidean; Patti, Rick & Jesse, unfortunately they were far away from us, in a marina on the other side of town. But Brian did spend some time with them and with Andy on Harmony. He may not see another kid for a long time. Spent an afternoon & evening with Ken & Larry on Julie. Really enjoyed their company. Saw Mike & Marguerite on Ithaca and paid them in person for the Autopilot control head they sent us. Met Leo on Moonlight again and did some computer work for the Europeans. More boats came in every day, so it was nonstop partying at the various marinas & sailing clubs in Darwin. Pretty tropical city, lots of palm trees. No rain at all in the month of July! Brian got his contact lenses but is having some trouble with them. Saw Harry Potter III and spent lots of money. After 2 days of parties, we are burnt out and happy to have a peaceful sail away from Australia. It has been a great 8½ months, we hate to leave, but Bali & the Indian Ocean are beckoning! Of course we also got to see Feel Free, Bedouin, and Tranquility. Brian got paid for helping them clean and paint their bottoms on the careening grid. We careened there also and slapped another coat of paint on — very handy.
